title: Breadth-First Search Explores by Distance
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Breadth-first search visits vertices in nondecreasing number of edges from the source, using a queue.
short: A FIFO queue processes the frontier one layer at a time.
long: A FIFO queue processes the frontier one layer at a time. Every vertex is enqueued once and every adjacency list is scanned once.
proof: The queue contains vertices at distance d followed by vertices at distance d+1, by induction on layers.
consequence: BFS yields shortest paths in unweighted graphs and the connected components of undirected graphs.

title: BFS Gives Unweighted Shortest Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In an unweighted graph, the parent pointers produced by BFS form shortest paths from the source to every reachable vertex.
short: First discovery is via a shortest route.
long: First discovery is via a shortest route. Edge weights can be handled by BFS only when all weights are equal or 0-1 BFS is used.
proof: If a shorter path existed, its penultimate vertex would be discovered in an earlier layer and would have enqueued v sooner.
consequence: BFS is the standard algorithm for hop-count distances and minimum-step puzzles.

title: DFS Discovery and Finish Times
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Depth-first search assigns discovery and finish times, and these intervals are either disjoint or nested.
short: DFS produces a nesting of recursive intervals.
long: DFS produces a nesting of recursive intervals. The parenthesis structure underlies topological sorting, SCC algorithms and bridge detection.
proof: A vertex is finished only after all descendants are finished, so intervals of descendant and non-descendant cannot partially overlap.
consequence: Finish-time order is a reusable primitive in many linear graph algorithms.

title: DFS Edge Classification in Directed Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: DFS classifies directed edges as tree, back, forward or cross according to the discovery and finish times of their endpoints.
short: Timestamps reveal cycles and ancestry.
long: Timestamps reveal cycles and ancestry. A directed graph is acyclic exactly when DFS finds no back edge.
proof: Edges to gray vertices are back edges, edges to descendants are forward edges, and edges to already finished non-descendants are cross edges.
consequence: The classification gives a linear cycle test and supports dependency analysis.

title: Topological Sort from DFS Finish Order
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting vertices by decreasing DFS finish time gives a topological order of a directed acyclic graph.
short: Finish later means depend on fewer predecessors.
long: Finish later means depend on fewer predecessors. Every edge u->v satisfies f(u) > f(v), so reversing finish time puts u before v.
proof: If u->v and u is discovered first, v finishes before u; if v is discovered first, the edge is a cross edge and v still finishes earlier.
consequence: It schedules tasks respecting precedence constraints in linear time.

title: Kahn's Algorithm for Topological Order
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly removing a vertex of in-degree zero and decreasing its neighbours' in-degrees yields a topological order, or detects a cycle.
short: Peel off vertices with no remaining prerequisites.
long: Peel off vertices with no remaining prerequisites. A queue or stack holds the current zero-in-degree set.
proof: A vertex can be output only after all predecessors are output, and in a DAG at least one zero-in-degree vertex exists at every step.
consequence: It is the standard implementation of dependency resolution and build ordering.

title: A Directed Graph Has a Topological Order iff It Is Acyclic
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A topological ordering exists for a directed graph if and only if the graph contains no directed cycle.
short: Cycles make precedence requirements impossible.
long: Cycles make precedence requirements impossible. A directed cycle requires each vertex on it to come before itself in any order.
proof: Necessity is immediate; sufficiency follows because a DAG always has a source, and induction removes it recursively.
consequence: Cycle detection and topological sorting are equivalent tasks.

title: Strongly Connected Components Partition a Digraph
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Strongly connected components are maximal vertex sets in which every vertex reaches every other, and they partition the vertices.
short: Mutual reachability is an equivalence relation.
long: Mutual reachability is an equivalence relation. Contracting components yields a directed acyclic graph, the condensation of the original graph.
proof: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of mutual reachability make it an equivalence relation whose classes partition V.
consequence: SCC decomposition simplifies analysis of reachability and cyclic dependencies.

title: Kosaraju's Two-Pass SCC Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Running DFS once on a digraph and then on its transpose in decreasing finish-time order identifies all strongly connected components in O(V+E) time.
short: Process the reversed graph in finish-time order.
long: Process the reversed graph in finish-time order. The first DFS on the transpose starting from the highest finish-time vertex isolates one source component of the condensation.
proof: Vertices of a component are discovered together in the second pass and no edge of the transpose leads outside before the component is complete.
consequence: It is a simple linear-time method for SCC decomposition.

title: Tarjan's Low-Link SCC Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A single DFS maintaining low-link values and a stack extracts each strongly connected component when its root is finished.
short: Back edges tell us when a DFS subtree closes into a component.
long: Back edges tell us when a DFS subtree closes into a component. low(v) is the smallest discovery time reachable from v via tree and at most one back edge.
proof: A component root has low-value equal to its own discovery time, so the stack segment above it forms exactly that component.
consequence: It computes SCCs in one pass without building the transpose.

title: Bridge Detection with Low Values
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In a DFS tree of an undirected graph, a tree edge (u,v) is a bridge exactly when low(v) > discovery(u).
short: No back edge from v's subtree reaches u or above.
long: No back edge from v's subtree reaches u or above. All non-tree edges in undirected DFS are back edges to an ancestor.
proof: If low(v) exceeds d(u), removing (u,v) separates v's subtree; otherwise a back edge provides an alternate route.
consequence: It finds vulnerable edges in networks in linear time.

title: Articulation Point Criterion
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In an undirected graph, a non-root DFS vertex u is an articulation point iff a child v satisfies low(v) >= discovery(u); the root is one iff it has more than one DFS child.
short: Cut vertices are detected by subtrees with no back route above them.
long: Cut vertices are detected by subtrees with no back route above them. The condition is evaluated during the same DFS that computes discovery and low values.
proof: If low(v) >= d(u), removing u disconnects v's subtree from the rest; the root separates each of its child subtrees.
consequence: It provides a linear-time test for network vulnerability.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm and Non-Negative Weights
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly settles the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges; it is correct when all edge weights are non-negative.
short: Greedy settlement is safe once no edge can reduce a settled distance.
long: Greedy settlement is safe once no edge can reduce a settled distance. With a Fibonacci heap the bound improves to O(E + V log V) amortised.
proof: If all weights are non-negative, any alternative path to the minimum tentative vertex via an unsettled vertex has length at least the current tentative distance.
consequence: It is the standard shortest-path method for road maps and network routing.

title: Dijkstra with a Binary Heap Complexity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Using a binary min-heap with decrease-key, Dijkstra runs in O((V+E) log V) time and O(V) extra space.
short: Each edge relaxation can cause a logarithmic heap update.
long: Each edge relaxation can cause a logarithmic heap update. With lazy duplicate insertions instead of decrease-key the bound becomes O(E log E), asymptotically comparable.
proof: There are at most E relaxations and V extract-mins, each costing O(log V).
consequence: This is the usual implementation choice for sparse graphs.

title: Dijkstra Fails on Negative Edges
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: With edges s->a of weight 1, s->b of weight 2 and b->a of weight -2, Dijkstra settles a at distance 1 and never corrects it to 0.
short: A settled vertex can later be reached more cheaply.
long: A settled vertex can later be reached more cheaply. Non-negativity is essential; Bellman-Ford handles negative edges but is slower.
proof: Dijkstra never reprocesses settled vertices, yet the path s-b-a has total weight 0 < 1.
consequence: Check edge signs before choosing a shortest-path algorithm.

title: Bellman-Ford and Negative Cycle Detection
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Relaxing all E edges V-1 times computes single-source shortest paths with negative edges, and one more pass detects a reachable negative cycle.
short: Repeated relaxation propagates improvements around cycles.
long: Repeated relaxation propagates improvements around cycles. If any distance still improves on the V-th pass, a negative cycle reachable from the source exists.
proof: A simple shortest path has at most V-1 edges, so after V-1 passes all distances are final unless a negative cycle permits endless improvement.
consequence: It is the method of choice when negative weights are possible and graphs are small or sparse.

title: Bellman-Ford Early Termination
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If a full relaxation pass makes no change, Bellman-Ford can stop before V-1 rounds.
short: No updates means the distances have converged.
long: No updates means the distances have converged. The best case is one pass plus a check, i.e. O(E), for favourable edge orderings.
proof: Once no edge can be relaxed, the distance labels satisfy the Bellman optimality conditions and are final.
consequence: Early exit makes Bellman-Ford competitive on many practical graphs.

title: SPFA Worst-Case Warning
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The short-path faster algorithm (SPFA), a queue-based Bellman-Ford variant, is often fast but has Theta(VE) worst-case running time.
short: Good average behaviour is not a worst-case guarantee.
long: Good average behaviour is not a worst-case guarantee. Specially constructed graphs force nearly every edge to be relaxed O(V) times.
proof: The queue-based ordering is still a form of repeated full relaxation, so the Bellman-Ford worst-case construction applies.
consequence: Use SPFA cautiously in latency-critical applications.

title: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths by allowing each vertex in turn as an intermediate point, taking O(V^3) time and O(V^2) space.
short: Intermediates are introduced one at a time.
long: Intermediates are introduced one at a time. It also detects negative cycles: a negative diagonal entry after the run signals one.
proof: After processing the first k vertices, d[i][j] is the shortest path whose internal vertices lie among those k; induction proves the update.
consequence: It is simple and fast enough for dense graphs of moderate size.

title: Floyd-Warshall In-Place Dynamic Program
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Floyd-Warshall recurrence needs only a single distance matrix because iteration k never changes entries already used for earlier intermediates.
short: The k-th row and column are reused during step k without a second matrix.
long: The k-th row and column are reused during step k without a second matrix. Predecessor matrices can be maintained alongside distances to reconstruct paths.
proof: Since intermediate k is new, the shortest path using it decomposes into two paths with smaller intermediates already finalised.
consequence: The algorithm's memory footprint is just quadratic in the number of vertices.

title: Johnson's Algorithm for Sparse Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Johnson reweights edges using potentials from one Bellman-Ford run, then runs Dijkstra from every vertex, taking O(VE + V^2 log V) time.
short: Make weights non-negative once, then reuse fast Dijkstra.
long: Make weights non-negative once, then reuse fast Dijkstra. The potential h(v)=dist(s,v) yields non-negative reduced weights w'(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(u)-h(v) when no negative cycle exists.
proof: The triangle inequality gives w'(u,v) >= 0, and reduced path costs differ from original ones only by endpoint potentials, preserving shortest paths.
consequence: It is asymptotically better than Floyd-Warshall on sparse graphs with possibly negative edges.

title: Shortest Paths in a DAG
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Relaxing edges in topological order computes single-source shortest paths in a directed acyclic graph in O(V+E) time, even with negative edge weights.
short: Topological order already respects every dependency.
long: Topological order already respects every dependency. Longest paths and critical-path analysis use the same recurrence with maximisation.
proof: When an edge u->v is relaxed, all paths into u have already been processed, so dist[u] is final.
consequence: DAGs admit faster and more general shortest-path algorithms than general graphs.

title: A* Optimality with Admissible Heuristics
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A* search returns an optimal path when the heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost.
short: Optimistic estimates cannot hide a better route.
long: Optimistic estimates cannot hide a better route. Runtime depends strongly on heuristic quality; with h = 0, A* degenerates to Dijkstra.
proof: Before expanding a node with optimal cost C, some node on an optimal path with estimate at most C would have smaller f-value, so A* expands it first.
consequence: Admissible heuristics such as Manhattan distance make grid pathfinding fast and correct.

title: A* Consistency Avoids Reopening
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If an A* heuristic satisfies h(u) <= c(u,v) + h(v) for every edge, the first time a node is expanded is optimal and no reopening is needed.
short: Consistency makes f-values monotone along paths.
long: Consistency makes f-values monotone along paths. Consistency implies admissibility but not conversely.
proof: Along any path, f-values are nondecreasing, so a node cannot later be reached with a smaller f-value.
consequence: Consistent heuristics simplify implementations and bound the number of expansions.

title: Bidirectional Search Reduces Frontier Size
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Searching simultaneously from the source and target can reduce explored nodes from O(b^d) to about O(b^{d/2}) when both directions are available.
short: Two shallower searches meet in the middle.
long: Two shallower searches meet in the middle. It requires reversible edges or symmetric state transitions and a reliable meeting test.
proof: Each side explores to depth d/2, so the number of generated states is roughly twice b^{d/2}.
consequence: It is used in route planning and puzzle solving to accelerate breadth-first searches.
